The committee recommends restructuring the first-year graduate
methods sequence beginning next academic year. This memo summarizes
the motivation for the change, the proposed structure, and the
timeline for faculty discussion and a vote at the September meeting.

The current sequence has been essentially unchanged for a decade.
In that time both the entering cohorts and the methodological
demands of the field have shifted: students arrive with stronger
programming backgrounds but more heterogeneous mathematical
preparation, and causal inference and computational methods now
occupy a much larger share of published empirical work.

## Proposed Structure

The committee proposes replacing the current two-term sequence with
three quarter-length courses. The first covers probability and
statistical theory at the current level. The second is reorganized
around the design-based view of causal inference, consolidating
material that is now scattered across electives. The third is a new
course on computational methods, including simulation, numerical
optimization, and reproducible workflows.

No additional teaching resources are required. The third course
absorbs an existing elective, and the rotation already includes
faculty prepared to teach each component.

## Timeline

We will circulate detailed syllabi over the summer and hold an open
discussion at the first faculty meeting of fall term. If the
proposal is approved at the September meeting, the new sequence
takes effect for the entering cohort the following year. Comments
before then are welcome and should be sent to any member of the
committee.
